newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 4.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- BT SEALS 20 BILLION DOLLAR MCI MERGER
British Telecom and MCI have announced terms for a merger.

The deal will involve BT buying the 80 percent of MCI that it does not already own for 12.2 billion stg. The merger will create a holding company called Concert, the name of the two groups' existing joint venture in corporate network management.

The deal is seen as particularly important to BT and its global ambitions, especially in the deregulated US domestic market. The giant merger will make British Telecom one of the largest telecommunications groups in the world. Shareholders in BT are to be paid a special dividend, expected to cost the company some 2 billion stg.
-- PUBLIC SPENDING WILL LIMIT SCOPE FOR TAX CUTS

Public spending targets expected to be set this week by government ministers are likely to severely limit the scope of the chancellor to implement tax reductions in the November budget. However it is thought that Kenneth Clarke might reduce income tax by 1p to 23p and increase the income band at which a rate of 20p tax becomes payable. There remains some discussion to be carried out before the spending levels for several major departments, including social security, are agreed.
-- DEUTSCHE TELEKOM IN ROW WITH INVESTMENT BANKERS

A row between Deutsche Telekom and US investment bank Goldman Sachs has resulted in the bank being excluded from a leading role as global co-ordinator in the planned flotation of stock in Deutsche Telekom associate Matav, a Hungarian telecoms group. The dispute relates to Goldman Sachs' line on the price of shares in Deutsche Telekom itself, to be floated soon. The bank believed that the price range set by the German company was too high for many institutional investors.
-- BUILDING SOCIETIES BILL WINS CROSS-PARTY SUPPORT

It is reported that Labour will support renewed efforts by the Treasury to press ahead with the introduction of a building societies bill aimed at removing restrictions on the range of services that currently can be offered by mutual societies. Such Labour support could allow the bill to be rushed through parliament in as little as half a day. A final draft of the bill is expected to be published by the Treasury in early December.
-- KVAERNER TO BUILD CHINA'S LONGEST BRIDGE

Cleveland Structural Engineering, a UK subsidiary of the Norwegian shipping and engineering group Kvaerner, has secured a 100 million-stg contract to build the longest suspension bridge in China. It is expected that Kvaerner will reveal details today of the project, which will involve the construction of a 1.4-km bridge over the Yangzte River. The announcement will coincide with a visit to Britain by leading Chinese official Li Lanqing,
the country's vice-premier.
-- EBRD FORECASTS FASTER ECONOMIC GROWTH

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development in its latest transition report forecasts that the Baltic states will experience an increase in economic growth next year. However, questions remain over the prognosis for the economies of Russia and the Ukraine. In central Europe much will depend on how these countries' western European export markets fare. The report also notes the continued need for better services to be developed in the field of banking, insurance and pension provision.
-- POLL SHOWS CITY OPPOSES OFFSHORE LIMITED LIABILITY

A KPMG poll if City firms has found a majority opposed to the formation by accountancy firms of offshore limited liability partnerships. According to KPMG, which opposes such a strategy, two-thirds of those questioned said such structures were unacceptable. Several firms are considering such offshore structures as a way of protecting the assets of partners from
litigation.
-- WARNING THAT EMU WOULD PUT TAX UP 5P

Oxford Economic Forecasting in a report published on Monday will warn that taking Britain into the single European currency could cost as much as 5p on the basic rate of income tax. Such a move would be required to offset the fall that would take place in UK interest rates to lower continental levels. Unless such action were taken, the country could suffer inflationary pressure that would drive it into a recession.
-- DIRECTORS WARNED OF IT NEEDS FOR EMU
A report to be published on Monday by the
Anglo/Dutch
computer services group CMG warns that many of
Britain's top

companies are underestimating the implications for information technology of the planned creation of a single European currency. Some companies could face bills of up to 30 million stg upgrading their systems to deal with a single currency. The survey also found that 83 percent of finance directors among the UK's top 350 companies favour a single currency.
-- GEHE CONSIDERS LLOYDS CHEMISTS BID

It is thought that Gehe of Germany will this launch a bid for Lloyds Chemists. The cash offer would exceed the value of a share offer for the company levelled by UniChem more than two weeks ago. An offer of as much as 525p per share is possible if Gehe wishes to deter UniChem from improving on its own offer. A bid, if it is to be made, must be detailed by Friday, a deadline set by the government on October 18.
